Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

title: Diagnosis as Percolation on an Evidence Graph: Root-Cause Recoverability in Network Fault Diagnosis
summary: Diagnosing failures from incomplete observations presents three challenges: determining whether sufficient evidence connects a possible cause to a symptom, distinguishing the true cause from plausible alternatives, and assessing when a diagnosis can be trusted. We introduce an evidence-graph framework that separates these challenges and uses percolation theory to analyze how missing information affects cause-symptom connectivity. In controlled simulations with an average degree of four, a giant connected component emerges when approximately 25% of evidence is retained, but a specific cause-alarm pair reaches 50% connectivity only after slightly more than half is retained. Even connectivity does not guarantee correct cause identification. We apply this framework to multi-LLM diagnosis of IEEE 802.11 packet captures. A final reconciliation pass improves evidence-grounding weighted F1 from 0.912 to 0.964, primarily by removing isolated citations rather than connecting previously separate evidence chains, consistently across three graph constructions. However, connectivity is not a reliable confidence measure: its association with diagnostic quality becomes statistically insignificant after controlling for capture length, citation count, within-capture dependence, and multiple comparisons. Further experiments show that directed and weighted edges help selectively, while simpler overlap measures or domain-specific methods sometimes perform better. These findings establish evidence graphs as a framework for separating evidence availability, causal distinguishability, and confidence reliability, while demonstrating that connected evidence alone cannot certify diagnostic correctness.

title: Consistency-Aware Map Generation at Multiple Zoom Levels Using Aerial Image
summary: The multi-level tiled map service is widely used and serves as a kind of digital infrastructure. These map tiles are usually rendered from vector data, whose update needs to walk or drive with professional equipment to check every points of interest. This leads to inconvenience and expensive cost in timely updating maps. Compared with vector data, aerial images are much easier and cheaper to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-level map generation framework that can automatically generate accurate and consistent maps with multiple zoom levels from aerial images. It consists of a level-aware map generator and a consistency-aware map generator. The level-aware map generator is able to generate accurate initial maps with realistic details for each zoom level. The consistency-aware map generator regards initial maps at each zoom level as a sequence and builds the connection between them, so as to guarantee content consistency between maps at different zoom levels. Furthermore, we collect a large-scale high-quality dataset called Multi-Level Map (MLM) for map generation at multiple zoom levels. Experiments on our MLM dataset show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art map generation methods on both comprehensive quantitative metrics and perceptual quality.

title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

title: Disentangling Magnetospheric and Colliding-Wind X-ray and Radio Emission in the Post-Mass-Transfer Magnetic Massive Binary Plaskett's Star
summary: Plaskett's star is an O+O binary system harboring a kG-order magnetic field associated with the broad-lined secondary. It is the only O-type star believed to host a centrifugally supported magnetosphere. We present orbital- and rotational-phase resolved X-ray and low-frequency radio observations of Plaskett's star. X-ray observations were taken with Chandra using the High Energy Transmission Grating Spectrometer (HETGS), while the radio observations come from uGMRT and VLA. The X-ray light curve shows rotational modulation according to the magnetic component's rotation period, with maximum flux near magnetic minima. We confirm the decline in flux near orbital phase 0.5 where the slow rotator primary is in front of its magnetic companion. We used the $f/i$ ratios of Si XIII and Mg XI from high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy to infer the location of the plasma emitting X-rays. We find no statistically significant variation in line widths or centroid shifts with either orbital or rotational phase; however, given instrumental limitations, this non-detection may partly reflect observational constraints, while still suggesting a complex and extended X-ray emitting plasma distribution. We could not detect the star in the low-frequency radio bands (0.6--1.5 GHz). Re-analysis of existing Very Large Array data reveals an additional detection at 3 GHz, consistent with a nonthermal contribution predicted by magnetospheric models, although no direct signature was obtained. At low frequencies, nonthermal emission from the magnetosphere and the colliding-wind region is likely suppressed by free-free absorption in the winds of one or both components.

title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
summary: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

title: Conditional Stochastic User Equilibrium as a Gibbs Distribution: Tractable Flow Laws and Exact Path-Free Sampling
summary: Treating traffic counts as data calls for the joint distribution of link flows. Stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) gives a single flow vector, and independent route choice at fixed probabilities ignores congestion feedback between travelers. Conditional stochastic user equilibrium (CSUE), in which each traveler of a finite population chooses a route by logit conditional on the routes of all others, contains this feedback but has been hard to compute with at scale. Under separable link costs and a common route-choice precision, the CSUE conditionals are those of a unique Gibbs distribution whose energy is a left-endpoint discrete congestion potential, and for continuous nondecreasing costs the law concentrates on deterministic logit SUE in the large-population limit. When the routes of each origin are the paths of an acyclic bush, retaining origin- or OD-level labels gives an unnormalized layered link-flow law with an explicit product-form multiplicity. On this representation we build a block Metropolis-Hastings sampler whose proposal is an integer version of Dial's loading under frozen costs. It leaves the CSUE law on the bush route sets invariant without enumerating paths or storing individual routes, and at stationarity the mean rejection rate of a block lies between one and two times the total variation distance between its proposal and exact conditional. In experiments, the sampler reproduces reference laws from exact enumeration and traveler-level Gibbs sampling, whereas independent route choice at frozen costs reproduces mean flows but overstates link-flow standard deviations by up to 48% and distorts correlations. On Sioux Falls, the block sampler attains 76.1 times the minimum effective sample size per CPU second of traveler-level Gibbs sampling, and on Chicago Sketch, with over one million travelers, its sampled covariance is used to assess traffic-count locations.

title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
summary: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $π_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.

title: Affordable Analytic Gradients for G0W0-BSE Excited States for Multiple GW Variants via Back-Propagation
summary: We derive, implement and validate analytic nuclear gradients for three variants of $GW$ self-energies---the contour-deformation (CD), the analytic continuation (AC), and the contour deformation with $W$-analytic-continuation (CD-WAC)---and for the Bethe--Salpeter equation (BSE) built on top of them. All gradients are expressed as contractions of a set of covectors connected to derivatives of primitive quantities in SCF calculations. The derivation of these covectors is a back-propagation procedure through the $GW$ and BSE equations. Central finite differences confirm the correctness of all implemented gradients. With the AC-$GW$-BSE gradient we optimize the excited-state geometries of carbon monoxide, a donor-acceptor dye labelled as DA1, and DMABN, a typical model system for twisted intramolecular charge-transfer phenomena (TICT), and have obtained results that successfully reproduce observations from experiments or high-level calculations. We also performed trajectory surface hopping (TSH) simulations of nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) of DMABN using the SHARC NAMD package, showing the capacity of our method to simulate NAMD problems. We performed timing and memory scaling tests, demonstrating that the gradient calculations of both $GW$ and BSE scale asymptotically as $N^4$ for timing and $N^3$ for memory. All source codes used in the present work, including the REST program package and the modified SHARC NAMD package that supports REST as the quantum chemistry backend, are available on Gitee https://gitee.com/restgroup/rest and https://gitee.com/qirui-gao-2025/sharc

title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
summary: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
summary:
Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_θ$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one.
  Code at: https://github.com/vicgalle/craftax-program-policies

title: On the Cauchy problem for $σ$-evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients via upper decay indicators
summary: In this paper, the first main goal is to investigate the Cauchy problem for the linear $σ$-evolution equation $$u_{tt}+a^2(t)(-Δ)^σu+b(t)u_t+m^2(t)u=0, $$ where propagation speed, damping term and mass are time-dependent functions. Under suitable assumptions on the interaction among these coefficients, we not only derive decay estimates for the solution and its derivatives in terms of the effective parabolic time scale $\mathcal{V}_{a,b}(s,t):=\int_s^t a^2(τ)/b(τ) dτ$, but also conclude the additional decay induced by the mass term and the upper decay indicators of the initial data. Especially, one can recognize that the time-derivative estimate for solutions exhibits a competition between $m^2(t)$ and $a^2(t)\left(1+\mathcal{V}_{a,b}(0,t)\right)^{-1}$. For the corresponding semi-linear problem with the nonlinear term $|u|^p$, we also establish global (in time) existence of small data solutions fulfilling decay estimates, coming from the mass factor $\exp\left(-\int_0^t m^2(τ)/b(τ)dτ\right)$, under the same assumptions on these coefficients.

title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

title: PathLoop: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Reasoning for Evidence-Grounded Whole-Slide Image Analysis
summary: Analyzing whole-slide images (WSIs) requires combining evidence across tissue regions and spatial scales. Multi-agent systems offer a promising approach to this task. However, existing systems make limited use of molecular evidence, often select visually prominent but less representative regions while overlooking global context, and struggle to reuse experience from previous cases. To address these challenges, we present PathLoop, a self-evolving multi-agent framework that integrates omics data for evidence-grounded WSI analysis. Specifically, PathLoop coordinates visual and omics interpreters across slide, patch, and pixel levels, using molecular signals to guide region selection and combining local tissue details with global slide features. A judgment agent then checks the consistency of the collected evidence against Pathology-Wiki, a knowledge base built from 48 entries across 24 organ systems, and triggers re-examination when the evidence is inconsistent. To reuse past experience, a four-level memory stores reasoning trajectories, practical tips, skills, and tools to guide future cases, forming a loop of evidence collection, review, and memory update. We evaluate PathLoop on four TCGA cohorts with biomarker prediction, survival prediction, and subtype classification. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of PathLoop across these tasks and support its use for evidence-grounded WSI analysis.

title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
summary: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

title: Scalable composite likelihood inference for directed probit networks
summary: We develop scalable estimation and inference for directed probit networks with correlated sending and receiving effects and residual reciprocity. An incomplete composite likelihood in two stages combines exact bivariate margins of sampled dyads and triples, avoiding integration in high dimensions and cubic enumeration. For fixed parameter dimension, criterion evaluation is linear in the number of draws. Averaging a fixed number of fits from independent index samples reduces sampling variation and allows parallel computation. We establish consistency and joint asymptotic normality with different directional rates, allowing a singular node projection when draw counts lie between the node and dyad scales. An overlap covariance accounts for network and index variation and is consistent relative to each directional variance. Independent index samples stabilize covariance estimation without refitting. The resulting procedure provides standard errors, mapped joint regions and score tests for zero variance components. Simulations show improved estimation from averaging and substantially lower computation times than default Bayesian fitting. An application to a fly brain network with 21,738 neurons demonstrates estimation and inference at a scale relevant to modern network data.

title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
summary: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

title: Latent Molecular Rollout Towards Causal World Models: Direction is Learnable, Amplitude Control is Readout-Dependent
summary:
A molecular world model should predict how structural changes alter physical properties, not merely assign labels to static molecules. We build a latent molecular rollout system on an 8B Qwen3 backbone, trained on 9,202 aqueous experimental pKa pairs from iBonD, and assess its progress toward causal control by auditing three often-conflated capabilities: predictive fidelity through the intended molecular pathway, directional learnability versus amplitude calibration of target-conditioned displacements, and transfer of latent control to decoded structures.
  After removing textual shortcuts, continuous latent inference achieves a test MAE of 2.087, significantly outperforming direct molecular feature readout (MAE difference -0.276, 95% CI [-0.352, -0.203], p<0.001). A target-conditioned policy reliably learns displacement directions, with a median cosine of 0.577 and 62.8% of 43 held-out pairs exceeding the 0.3 threshold.
  Amplitude conclusions are strictly readout-dependent. A frozen linear readout yields near-zero amplitude correlation (-0.020), while a nonlinear gradient-based readout recovers relative amplitude ordering (correlation 0.585, sign accuracy 0.744-0.767) with compressed absolute scale.
  At the decoded structure level, neither input-slot editing nor direct final-state injection produces meaningful changes across 80 test sources, bounding the tested control surfaces rather than indicating a universal decoder bottleneck. Generation fine-tuning shows relative improvement under internal oracle evaluation but does not surpass a simple constant baseline in single-sample settings.
  These results delineate the capability frontier of fixed-scale latent molecular interfaces: directional control is robustly achievable, but calibrated amplitude control and decoded structural transfer remain open challenges on the path to causal molecular world models.

title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
summary: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo 3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3 % accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1 %). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1 % and 89.6 %, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

title: Beyond Paired Inputs: Learning to Leverage RGB-T Cross-Modal Relations in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

title: Unbound matter in the circum-halo medium: a common mediator of halo secondary bias
summary: Halo secondary bias describes the dependence of halo clustering on properties beyond mass. Here we report that a new environmental metric, the unbound matter fraction ($f_{\rm un}$) in the $2$--$3\,R_{\rm vir}$ shell around a halo, can largely account for secondary bias. Using haloes with $M_{\rm vir}=10^{10.5}$--$10^{14.5}h^{-1}{\rm M_\odot}$ at $z=0$ obtained from TNG300-1-Dark, we find that controlling for $f_{\rm un}$ reduces the secondary bias of formation time, concentration, spin, shape and velocity anisotropy to a residual correlation of $\lesssim 4\%$, outperforming other environmental metrics such as the tidal anisotropy for spin and velocity anisotropy. Applying a stacking method to the circum-halo medium (CHM), we identify two distinct flow patterns: low-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes co-move with coherent flows, with the CHM converging onto the haloes; in contrast, high-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes move through dynamically hot, partially virialized structures, with the CHM passing by rather than being accreted. This dichotomy points to two distinct regimes of secondary bias, a `cold' regime and a `hot' regime, in which tidal and inertial forces act as the main drivers, respectively, with the dominant mechanism migrating from the former to the latter as haloes assemble into massive structures. At fixed large-scale environment, $f_{\rm un}$ further indicates the presence of nearby neighbours and the competitive accretion. Our results highlight the role of unbound matter as a mediator of environmental effects on haloes, and reveal the physical mechanisms that shape the CHM pattern through which these effects are mediated.

title: Self-similarity of axisymmetric Marangoni flows on a deep viscous subphase
summary: Local gradients of surface tension caused by inhomogeneous distributions of surfactant molecules are known to generate Marangoni flows, the mechanics of which have important consequences in various areas of science and engineering. In this paper, we investigate the deposition of insoluble surfactants on the surface of a deep, viscous subphase, which propagate axisymmetrically without diffusing. We study these flows from the perspective of self-similarity, i.e., seeking solutions which show universal features on appropriate length and time scales. We first present a closed form, self-similar solution of the first kind for the axisymmetric spreading of surfactants, which is globally valid at long times. We then numerically study `filling' flows of surfactant, where the surfactant distribution is locally depleted such that inward flows are generated to `fill' the surfactant-free area. These flows have the special feature of forming cusp-like structure in finite time, which have been studied extensively in the literature of self-similarity of the second kind. We show that these flows admit a countably infinite number of stable similarity solutions based on the local behavior of the initial surfactant concentration profile. We remark on a few unique features of these results in contrast to filling flows in other physical limits.

title: PALIN: Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR Multimodal 3D Object Detection with Benchmark
summary: 3D object detection is critical for intelligent transportation systems. LiDAR has been widely adopted for accurate geometric measurements; however, purely geometric representations remain ambiguous under sparse observations and occlusions, while cross-sensor multimodal fusion suffers from calibration and synchronization errors. To overcome these challenges, we leverage an Ouster LiDAR to construct PALIN (Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR), a large-scale intrinsically pixel-aligned multimodal dataset jointly capturing geometry and NIR intensity, comprising approximately 8,000 annotated frames from static urban intersections and diverse mobile suburban scenes. Building upon this dataset, we propose CMambaFusion, a novel fusion framework consisting of a four-directional Cross-Mamba module for bidirectional cross-modal interaction and a Gated Concat-Mamba module for joint feature refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PALIN enables effective multimodal learning, and CMambaFusion achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over both LiDAR-only and representative fusion baselines.

title: Computing rare events in Lévy-driven systems via optimal control
summary: We extend the optimal control formulation of sample path large deviation theory, which has proven effective for numerical computation of instantons and sharp probability estimates in stochastic differential equations with Gaussian noise, to systems with light-tailed Lévy noise. In the scaling limit of small jumps and high intensity, such systems satisfy a large deviation principle of Freidlin-Wentzell type, with a running cost given by the Legendre transform of the noise cumulant generating function. We propose to numerically minimize this cost over noise realizations subject to the system dynamics, which yields the instanton without having to solve Hamilton's equations, and naturally handles degenerate and multiplicative noise. When the cumulant generating function has a bounded domain, the cost grows only linearly for large noise, and instantons can contain jumps. We analyze when jumps are not only admissible but optimal, depending on the subleading behavior of the cost and on the drift, and show how jumps can be resolved numerically through a time reparameterization that freezes physical time. For continuous instantons, we derive Riccati and Fredholm determinant expressions for the leading-order prefactor, and we discuss the modifications needed when the instanton jumps. We illustrate and validate our methods against Monte Carlo simulations in several examples: a two-dimensional nonlinear model, an active run-and-tumble particle with non-Gaussian tumbling noise, and the Ghil-Sellers energy balance climate model with Lévy-perturbed solar forcing.

title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
summary: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

title: Local asymptotic normality for Cox-Ingersoll-Ross drift parameters under high-frequency sampling and the strict Feller condition
summary: For the ergodic Cox--Ingersoll--Ross (CIR) diffusion with known diffusion scale and a fixed initial value, we prove local asymptotic normality (LAN) of the exactly sampled experiment for the drift parameters whenever the Feller index exceeds $1$, assuming only a vanishing mesh and a diverging observation horizon. This improves the previously known condition that the index exceed $(11+\sqrt{89})/2$. The proof cuts off the continuous score near $0$, recovers the remainder by exact conditional centering on each sampling interval, and transfers LAN by a conditional-likelihood argument.

title: Generic finiteness of rotating relative equilibria in the planar $N$-vortex problem
summary: For every $N\ge2$, we prove that Zariski-generic nonzero real circulations, with any prescribed signs, admit at most $N^{2N}$ labeled, collision-free rotating relative equilibria modulo translations, rotations in $SO(2)$, and positive scaling. The excluded parameters lie in an explicit finite union of quadratic hypersurfaces. The proof combines a logarithmic-residue obstruction to positive-dimensional complex solution sets with Bézout degree bounds.

title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
summary: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

title: InvarOrd: Self-Supervised Ordinal Knowledge Distillation with Rank-Invariant Alignment for Label-Efficient Cross-Species Hyperspectral Fish Freshness Assessment
summary: Hyperspectral models of fish freshness rarely transfer between species, and labelling a new species is slow and destructive. Freshness is also ordinal, and standard domain alignment can erase that order. We present InvarOrd, which adapts to a new species from 30 labelled cubes (5 per rank) in three stages: self-supervised spectral pretraining on unlabelled source cubes, cross-species alignment by a shrinkage covariance discrepancy computed only within matched ranks, and ordinal distillation into a compact student. The alignment term is provably invariant to the rank means, so it gives no incentive to collapse the ordinal axis. On paired salmon and cod data (800 cubes each, 16 days), a source-trained teacher reaches 1.6 to 1.9 days mean absolute error (MAE) on the other species, with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) below zero. The 423K-parameter student, 2.54 times smaller than its teacher, attains the lowest MAE (1.476 days) and highest within 1-day accuracy (56.1%) among 14 configurations, matching the best of six ImageNet-pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-T, 1.503 days) at 66 times fewer parameters, 1.44ms per cube on a GPU and 5s re-adaptation. InvarOrd beats target-only training by 0.29 days (p = 0.031). Among alignment objectives, rank-invariant alignment retains the most ordinal structure (embedding rank correlation 0.183, QWK 0.112), whereas global discrepancy lowers the rank correlation to 0.049 and QWK to zero at only 0.014 days higher MAE.

title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
summary:
Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition.
  On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
summary: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

title: Fluctuation modes in the initial state of heavy-ion collisions: from 2D to 3D hybrid simulations
summary: This dissertation investigates how the initial stages of relativistic heavy-ion collisions shape the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and the observables measured experimentally. Particular attention is given to the initial state and pre-equilibrium dynamics, which constitute the main sources of uncertainty in hybrid simulations. The first part of the dissertation reviews the framework underlying state-of-the-art hybrid simulations and the numerical tools used in phenomenological analyses. The second part studies the matching between pre-equilibrium evolution and viscous hydrodynamics. Since commonly used conformal kinetic-theory descriptions are inconsistent with the non-conformal hydrodynamic equation of state, an entropy-density matching prescription is proposed. This prescription reduces the artificial bulk pressure generated at the switching time and improves the consistency of the hybrid framework. The third part develops a mode-by-mode decomposition of initial energy-density profiles to isolate fluctuation modes and quantify their contributions to final observables. Applied to Pb-Pb collisions across centrality classes and extended to a fully three-dimensional O-O collision system, the method shows that initial fluctuations survive hydrodynamic evolution and leave measurable imprints on final observables. In O-O collisions, fluctuations can dominate over geometric effects from the impact parameter, demonstrating that intermediate-sized systems are not simply scaled-down versions of large systems. Overall, these results provide tools for constraining the early stages of heavy-ion collisions and for understanding how fluctuations propagate through the QGP evolution.

title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
summary: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

title: CLEW: Log-Anchored Backward Tracing for Root-Cause Code Localization
summary: Failures in industrial software systems may involve multiple components and be difficult to reproduce outside the production environment. Root-cause code localization therefore often relies on issue descriptions and runtime logs. However, log evidence may be noisy or incomplete, and the code reporting a symptom may differ from the code containing the underlying defect. These conditions make it challenging to identify relevant log evidence and determine which functions could have caused the reported failure. To address this gap, we introduce CLEW, an agentic approach that combines rule-based log-to-code anchoring with LLM-guided backward code tracing. CLEW organizes selected observations into diagnostic states, guides source exploration from anchored symptom functions, and returns ranked candidate functions, an affected module, and an explanation comprising a proposed mechanism path and associated log events. For evaluation, we construct LogLoc, a benchmark comprising 192 real-world issue and fault-injection cases. Against three baselines, CLEW records the highest observed Acc@1 (77.3%) and MRR (81.3%) on LogLoc-Issues and matches the leading baselines at 97.6% Acc@1 on LogLoc-Airflow. Averaged over all 192 cases, CLEW's wall-clock time is approximately 73% lower than LocAgent's at a similar average inference cost. No aggregate degradation is observed under the tested perturbations, with modest changes in Acc@1 and MRR across the evaluated seeds and base models. These results suggest that CLEW can combine function-level localization with evidence links and runtime efficiency under the evaluated conditions.

title: Low-energy spectral-window truncation for compact U(1) lattice gauge theory
summary: We establish a nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound covering the entire vacuum-relative low-energy spectral window of the original pure compact $U(1)$ lattice Hamiltonian. Formulated on a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice with $N\geq3$ sites per direction at $θ=0$ in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector, our factorial-squared tail-norm estimate applies uniformly to every normalized vector in the window without requiring physical eigenvalue isolation, a window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy, and carries no window-dimension factor. This uniform control bounds ordered low-energy eigenvalue and excitation-energy errors while governing finite-time hard-wall evolution initialized from each state's normalized projection. Within this model, an analytic finite-volume strong-coupling construction certifies a nonvacuum band and an order-one coherent plaquette signal change that persists under a specified finite cutoff. The window estimate further provides precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs, a polar-decomposition linear isometric encoding for reference-entangled inputs, and readout bounds for the local electric square. Under lattice refinement at fixed positive bare coupling, physical volume, window width, and evolution duration, cutoffs scaling as $β\log N/\log\log N$ with $β>2$ drive the state and bounded-readout truncation errors to zero.

title: GRASP: Query-Adaptive Graph Retrieval framework with Cross-Attention Scoring and Path Sufficiency Verification for Question Answering
summary: Retrieval quality is a key factor in the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), particularly when retrieval is performed over structured knowledge graphs. Graph-based retrieval requires decisions about candidate-edge scoring, traversal termination, and the sufficiency of the retrieved evidence. We propose GRASP, a query-adaptive graph retrieval framework that jointly addresses these decisions during the retrieval process. A cross-attention scorer models fine-grained interactions between individual query tokens and candidate edges, providing query-specific signals for edge selection. A learned stopping gate conditions traversal termination on the query, traversal state, and hop depth, allowing the retrieval depth to adapt to the current retrieval state. A sufficiency classifier further evaluates the assembled path before generation and triggers re-retrieval when the evidence is predicted to be incomplete. We evaluate GRASP on three biomedical question-answering benchmarks with different graph scales and answer lengths, using biomedical question answering as a representative setting for evaluating graph-based RAG retrieval. GRASP consistently improves over the strongest learned baseline across the evaluated retrieval and generation metrics. The unsupported-claim rate is reduced by 8.9% to 13.2% across the three benchmarks, with the largest reduction on the benchmark with the longest generated answers. The retrieval gains are more pronounced under higher candidate density, while ablation results indicate that the three components provide complementary improvements.

title: Do Rule-Based Tools Help LLMs Translate Endangered Uralic Languages in the Prompt or over MCP?
summary: Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya and Udmurt have mature rule-based resources, among them finite-state analysers, constraint grammars and bilingual dictionaries, which language models do not use. We ask whether giving a model access to these resources improves machine translation from the four languages into English, and whether it matters how the access is provided: as analyses computed in advance and written into the prompt, or as tools that the model calls itself through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We evaluate manually: an expert linguist read every English output of the strongest model under three conditions, 816 sentences in all, accepted or rejected each one, and named the main error in every rejected translation. With the analyses in the prompt, the number of accepted translations rises from 13 to 43 out of 272; with the tools attached it rises to 55. The gain comes from the bilingual dictionary. For Udmurt, whose dictionary has no English side, the prompt-based condition brings no gain at all, while for the other three languages an English gloss reaches the prompt for 74 to 80% of the source words. Tool calling is also much harder to get working than prompt injection. Of 31 open-weight models, 14 never call a tool, 11 of them because they cannot produce a usable call, and half of the calls that are made name a language the toolkit does not support. We release the data set, every model output and all tool-call logs.

title: Radial Evolution of a Corotating Interaction Region from a High-Resolution MHD Simulation
summary: Corotating interaction regions (CIRs) are large-scale structures formed by fast--slow solar wind interaction, playing a crucial role in heliospheric dynamics and space weather. However, the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood. We investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR using a high-resolution simulation combined with a backmapping method. The simulation reproduces the major plasma and magnetic signatures observed by Wind at 1~AU and by MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at $\sim$1.6~AU. The CIR exhibits a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet, consistent with theoretical predictions. During its developing stage, geometric changes are modest, and the radial scalings of velocity ($V_r \propto r^{0.02}$), density ($N \propto r^{-2.00}$), magnetic field ($B_{\rm total} \propto r^{-1.74}$), and temperature ($T \propto r^{-0.97}$) are comparable to those of the background solar wind. In the mature stage, the CIR drifts in longitude and expands toward high latitudes, while its longitudinal and latitudinal widths decrease with distance. The full-domain scalings change markedly to $V_r \propto r^{0.13}$, $N \propto r^{-1.91}$, $B_{\rm total} \propto r^{0.35}$, and $T \propto r^{-0.52}$, differing from both the background wind and the ecliptic-plane CIR. This study quantifies the radial evolution of a CIR from formation to maturity and highlights the importance of its three-dimensional structure in characterizing its morphology and dynamics.

title: Cluster-Robust Inference in Small Samples Using Bias Corrections
summary: This paper derives an exact expression for the bias of the linearized estimator of the variance for cluster-robust inference, which generalizes an earlier result derived by Bell and McCaffrey (2002). Both cases of continuous and binary treatments are discussed. Under the former it is shown that the bias of the linearized variance estimator and its jackknife variant are of order $G^{-1}$ relative to the true variance, where $G$ denotes the total number of clusters. A bias-corrected variance estimator (BCCV) is then proposed and shown to have a relative bias of order $G^{-2}$. In the case of models with binary treatments the orders of the bias of standard estimators and the proposed bias-corrected one are shown to be $\max (G_{1}^{-1},G_{0}^{-1})$ and $\max (G_{1}^{-2},G_{0}^{-2})$, where $G_{1}$ and $G_{0}=G-G_{1}$ are the numbers of treated and untreated clusters. Scale and degrees of freedom adjustments to the $t$-statistic computed using bias-corrected standard errors are also proposed. Small sample properties of the proposed BCCV test are investigated using Monte Carlo experiments. It is shown that the proposed test generally outperforms tests based on conventional and jackknife cluster standard errors, and performs comparably to wild bootstrap inference and the recent jackknife distribution-adjusted testing procedure by \cite{hansen2026jackknife}. The utility of the proposed test is illustrated\ using three empirical applications from the literature.

title: From Objective Compromise to Structure-Enabled Intelligence: Reshaping the Scientific Paradigm of AI
summary: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are fundamentally constructed upon the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm. This paradigm can be characterized as an ill-posed optimization problem within a high-dimensional parameter space. When confronted with real-world scenarios characterized by noise and conflicting constraints, the logic of global error minimization inherently induces a strong smoothing effect. Consequently, this yields statistical compromise solutions that flatten local features, making it arduous to overcome the inherent bottleneck of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing AI models generate outputs purely based on statistical probabilities. They lack the capacity to autonomously discern truth from falsehood or establish causal logic, thereby lacking genuine cognitive intelligence. To address the ontological limitations of the OD paradigm, this paper proposes a novel paradigm termed \textit{Structure-Enabled Intelligence}. This approach abandons the conventional path of relying solely on computing power scaling and data fitting to achieve emergent intelligence. Instead, it embeds mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as underlying priors into the algorithmic architecture, constraining the model's solving process with structured scientific rules. Through this paradigm shift from ``data-driven objective fitting'' to ``mechanism-structure dominance,'' the proposed approach fundamentally mitigates the issue of statistical compromise, enhances the model's extrapolation and generalization capabilities, and simultaneously reshapes human-AI synergy by upholding human subjectivity in scientific cognition.

title: DyTransRM: A Unified Simulation-to-Real Framework for Dynamic Radio Map Prediction
summary: Dynamic radio map (RM) prediction enables proactive wireless network control by forecasting future propagation conditions from historical observations. However, collecting temporally continuous and spatially dense real-world RMs is prohibitively expensive, while models trained on large-scale simulated data often suffer from limited transferability to real environments. To address this issue, we propose DyTransRM, a unified simulation-to-real framework for dynamic RM prediction under sparse real-world measurements. DyTransRM first introduces RadioCLIP to learn physics-semantic representations by aligning environmental evolution with the corresponding propagation evolution, thereby improving both prediction accuracy and cross-domain transferability. To further bridge the simulation-to-real gap, SparseUOT employs sparse-mask simulation refinement to mimic realistic measurement patterns and unbalanced optimal transport to selectively align compatible propagation representations across domains. Experiments on RadioMapMotion and real-world datasets demonstrate that RadioCLIP achieves an NMSE of 0.0018 and an RMSE of 0.012 in simulation-domain prediction. After sparse real-domain adaptation, DyTransRM achieves an NMSE of 0.023, RMSE of 0.079, and MAE of 0.064, outperforming representative adaptation baselines without requiring spatially complete real RMs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DyTransRM for transferring simulation-learned dynamic propagation knowledge to practical sparse-measurement scenarios.

title: Hydrogen in Practice: A Global Review of Demonstration Projects from Production to Integration
summary: Hydrogen technology has the potential to address various challenges related to integrating low- and zero-carbon energy sources, as well as achieving carbon neutrality. It provides valuable solutions for transitioning to net-zero emission energy systems on a global scale. The implementation of hydrogen production and integration demonstration projects has received significant attention around the world and strong support from governments, highlighting the crucial role of such initiatives in the advancement of hydrogen energy. However, research in this area remains limited, particularly in terms of comprehensive and systematic reviews of industrial practices under real-world conditions. To bridge this gap, this article provides an in-depth review of hydrogen production, storage, and industrial applications, summarizing key features of thirteen exemplary hydrogen demonstration projects from around the world. The goal is to offer insights and guidance for the large-scale deployment of hydrogen energy while identifying potential technological pathways for the future.

title: Food co-purchasing networks encode geographic disparities in cardiometabolic health
summary: Unhealthy diets are a major driver of cardiometabolic disease, yet the geospatial structure of dietary behavior and its links to population health remain poorly understood. While large-scale retail transaction data offer a unique view of population dietary behavior, conventional approaches reduce purchases to isolated items, not accounting for how foods are actually combined. Here, we analyze 51 million grocery receipts across 95 Danish municipalities using a statistically validated bipartite network framework to isolate co-purchases that product popularity alone cannot explain. We find that, although municipalities buy largely the same products, their co-purchasing networks reorganize along a continuous urban-to-peripheral gradient in how those products are combined. The network backbone can be resolved into modular dietary communities whose local cohesion allows us to predict cardiometabolic prescriptions, explaining a quarter to a half of the variance left after sociodemographic adjustment, beyond what product prevalence alone accounts for. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) show no spatial gradient in prevalence and are located at the network periphery, where they share baskets with fresh foods but rarely form the combinations that hold the network together. Taken together, our findings show that geographic dietary differences are encoded not only in what people purchase, but in how foods are systematically combined within shopping baskets, offering a scalable network approach for population nutritional epidemiology.

title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
summary: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

title: Real-World End-to-End Product Entity Resolution
summary: Product Entity Resolution (PER) in e-commerce is challenging due to unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences. We present an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot PER pipelines---Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade---across established benchmarks and introduce two real-world datasets characterized by cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. We evaluate lexical and dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and Large Language Model verification, considering accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption.

title: Universal Analytical Description of Magnetoexcitons in Two-Dimensional Semiconducting Materials
summary: Matching the Coulomb and logarithmic limits of the Rytova--Keldysh model gives a universal zero-field spectrum for monolayer exciton $s$ states, $E_n\simeq-\mathrm{Ry}^*/[n-1/2+f_n(ξ)]^2$, where $ξ$ is the screening parameter. Analytical radii determine diamagnetic coefficients and the magnetic crossover scale. Zero-field deviations peak near $1\%$ across the full screening range $0\leqξ\leq100$. For the sampled hBN-encapsulated monolayers, magnetoexciton energies agree with numerical spectra to sub-meV rms up to $100\T$ and capture the measured orbital shifts. Shared parameters link optical and magneto-optical spectra.

title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
summary: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

title: Neural Surrogates for Tabulated Nuclear Equations of State in Core-Collapse Supernova Simulations
summary: Large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations rely on tabulated nuclear equations of state (EOSs), whose memory requirements can become a practical constraint in massively parallel calculations. We explore a compact alternative by replacing the tabulated thermodynamic mapping with a neural-network surrogate, using the Lattimer--Swesty EOS as a representative reference model. The surrogate directly predicts pressure, sound speed, and effective adiabatic index from $(\log ρ, \log e, Y_e)$ and accurately reconstructs the nonlinear thermodynamic structure of the EOS, including its behavior across phase-transition regions. It reproduces one-dimensional shock-tube solutions with hydrodynamic errors at the $\sim 10^{-3}$ level under different thermodynamic conditions and yields hydrostatic equilibrium configurations closely matching those obtained with the reference EOS. We find that smaller regression errors do not necessarily yield better hydrodynamic performance, demonstrating the importance of hydrodynamic validation in surrogate model selection. A compact network with only $\sim 10^4$ parameters retains this accuracy while reducing the memory required to store the EOS from $\sim 160$ MB to $\sim 100$ KB, corresponding to a reduction by a factor of $\sim 1500$. The surrogate also remains stable through collapse, bounce, shock formation, and post-bounce evolution in a one-dimensional adiabatic core-collapse calculation. These results demonstrate the potential of compact neural EOS surrogates for reducing memory requirements in large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations.

title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
summary: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

title: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation
summary: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.

title: Finite-size scaling of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking decoupled from thermodynamic criticality in a complex-conjugate Ising model
summary: We study a two-dimensional anisotropic Ising model with complex-conjugate couplings. Analytic continuation of the exact anisotropic Ising critical condition yields a candidate thermodynamic critical line, which is independently supported by finite-size scaling confirming the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Exact diagonalization of the transfer matrix and finite-size extrapolation reveal that the spectrum becomes complex, defining a separate $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry-breaking boundary in the thermodynamic limit. We find $K_{\rm PT}<K_c$ throughout the parameter range studied, leaving an intermediate regime with a complex spectrum while the system remains thermodynamically disordered. The spatial correlations remain short-ranged at $K_{\rm PT}$, in contrast to the critical correlations at $K_c$, directly distinguishing the spectral transition from thermodynamic criticality. The complex-conjugate anisotropy modifies the finite-size free-energy amplitude, and accounting for the corresponding anisotropy factor recovers the Ising central charge $c=1/2$. These results demonstrate that spectral $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking can occur without thermodynamic criticality, establishing a decoupling between spectral and thermodynamic transitions in a two-dimensional non-Hermitian statistical system.

title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
summary: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed.
